Judge rules seriously ill boy, 13, can be treated against mothers beliefs

Would LOVE to hear opinions on this one. Saved a life? Violated a woman and her child's beliefs? What's your opinion?

If violating your religious beliefs (providing you have religious beliefs) would save your life, would you? What if someone forced it upon you? Glad they saved you? Or angry you've been forced to sin (or w/e)?

Long winded opinionated opinion:

Seems to me that the child's beliefs differed from his mother's. (According to the article, at least) And considering that refusing to consent might well have resulted in his death, I don't think the mother had a right to contravene his wishes, even though he is a minor. I have teenaged boys. They are old enough to have this explained to them and for them to have informed consent, IMO. This is not a parent making a decision on behalf of an incapacitated (or very young) child. A child of this age most definitely should have a say in whatever medical treatments they may be subjected to, so long as everything is explained to them in a way that they can understand.

I am an atheist, so I have no religious beliefs to violate in that sense. The only thing I ask is that there not be extraordinary measures when there is little or no hope of saving me and/or it would not significantly improve the quality of my remaining life to intervene. I have a living will, and all my family members know what those wishes are as well.

Best thing you can do to be assured your wishes are followed is to have a living will, a person who is your medical POA who will make sure your wishes are honored, AND discuss it with your doctor as well. It only gets complicated, IMO, when you're dealing with minor children (especially those too young to really --not legally, as there is a difference-- consent to treatment and must rely on their parents/guardians to act in their best interests. Or in the case of adult children who are under the guardianship of their parents or other responsible parties because of mental disability or other conditions that render their ability to truly provide informed consent.
